items.stem: Which wireless security standard should a business prefer today where devices support it?

options.rationale: Correct: WPA3 offers the strongest current protections for Wi-Fi.
WEP is broken and must not be used.
An open network is unencrypted; hiding the SSID is not security.
WPA with TKIP is outdated and weaker than WPA2/WPA3.

items.explanation: Correct: WPA3 is the strongest widely available Wi-Fi standard.

items.stem: Which TWO signs suggest a rogue or evil-twin access point? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A familiar SSID appearing with a different or stronger signal unexpectedly
options.rationale: Correct: a duplicated SSID with odd signal is a classic evil-twin sign.

options.text: An access point with an unknown MAC on the corporate channel
options.rationale: Correct: unknown hardware broadcasting your network is suspicious.

options.text: A client device asking to join the network
options.rationale: Join requests are normal client behaviour.
A backup job is unrelated to rogue access points.

items.explanation: Correct: a duplicated SSID and an unknown broadcasting MAC both indicate a rogue AP.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Why should guest Wi-Fi be separated from business systems?

options.text: So a compromised guest device cannot reach sensitive internal systems
options.rationale: Correct: separation contains guest-side risk away from critical assets.

options.text: Because guests need faster speeds than staff
options.rationale: Speed is not the security rationale for separation.
Separation does not remove the need for encryption.

options.text: Because guests cannot use Wi-Fi otherwise
options.rationale: Guests can use shared networks; separation is about risk, not capability.

items.explanation: Correct: segmentation keeps guest-device compromise away from business systems.
